1.referenceTitle: The Non-GMO Project and the Non-GMO Project Verified mark
1.citation: The Non-GMO Project. About the Non-GMO Project: mission and history. Organization website, accessed 15 September 2026.
1.summary: The organization describes its origins in two grocery stores, their joint founding of the Project in 2007, and the arrival of the first Butterfly-labeled products on shelves in 2010. It presents the mark as certification for GMO avoidance and describes its growth as rapid.
1.establishes: This first-party history supports the launch date and the program’s stated purpose. Its growth description is promotional self-reporting; it does not supply an audited comparison with USDA Organic, establish why shoppers chose the mark, or show that the Butterfly alone caused its growth.
1.relevance: The history supplies the concrete example behind this briefing’s analogy between a focused non-GMO mark and a focused heavy-metal mark. Applying that example to HMTc is a positioning argument, not evidence that HMTc will achieve similar recognition or that the heavy-metal category has no competing marks.

2.citation: United States. Organic Foods Production Act of 1990, Pub. L. 101-624, title XXI, enacted 28 November 1990, codified at 7 U.S.C. §§6501–6524 (2024 edition). U.S. Department of Agriculture, National Organic Program, 7 C.F.R. Part 205. USDA Agricultural Marketing Service, The Organic Integrity Quarterly, October 2012, pp. 1–2.
2.summary: The 1990 Act created a national framework for organic production and handling, certification and labeling. USDA’s implementing standards were fully implemented in October 2002. The rules govern farming and handling practices, allowed substances, inspections, residue testing and use of the organic label.
2.establishes: Organic certification verifies compliance with this production-and-handling system; it is not a general guarantee that finished foods are free of metals. The system nevertheless expressly addresses heavy-metal contamination prevention in soil-fertility management and provides for residue testing and contaminant reporting. Its scope should not be described as wholly silent on metals.
2.relevance: These sources establish the federal framework against which the briefing compares the later Non-GMO Project mark. They help distinguish an organic production claim from HMTc’s claim about measured concentrations, but do not establish universal shopper trust in 1990 or HMTc’s commercial ownership of a category.

links.label: Organic Foods Production Act · U.S. Code

3.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Total Diet Study Report: Fiscal Years 2018–2020 Elements Data. July 2022.
3.summary: FDA measured nutrient and contaminant elements in retail foods, generally prepared for consumption. Its national monitoring results document detectable arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury in parts of the food supply.
3.establishes: These are food-surveillance data, not a comparison of organic and conventional farming or verification of a particular brand. A nondetect means below the analytical reporting limit, not demonstrated absence. FDA does not take regulatory action from these composited TDS results.
3.relevance: The occurrence data explain why an organic or non-GMO label cannot by itself report a product’s measured metal concentrations. They support the briefing’s rationale for concentration evidence, while providing no comparison of certification-market positions, no measure of demand for HMTc, and no finding that farming practices never influence contamination.

4.referenceTitle: Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist
4.citation: Supreme Court of the United States. Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist, No. 24-724, 607 U.S. ___, decided 24 February 2026. California AB 899, Chapter 668, Statutes of 2023, adding Health and Safety Code §110962. Maryland Rudy’s Law, HB 97 / SB 723 (2024), codified at Health–General §21-330.4. U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Reform, Subcommittee on Economic and Consumer Policy. Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury. Staff report, 4 February 2021.
4.summary: This grouped reference combines a unanimous Supreme Court ruling about federal jurisdiction in a baby-food lawsuit, California and Maryland baby-food testing and disclosure laws, and a congressional staff investigation of company testing records. Each addresses a different part of public scrutiny and accountability.
4.establishes: Palmquist resolved jurisdiction rather than product injury or liability. California phased in testing in 2024 and disclosure in 2025; Maryland phased them in during 2025 and 2026, within each law’s defined scope. The House report makes findings and recommendations. None measures demand for a heavy-metal seal or requires HMTc certification.
4.relevance: The materials explain the legal and public-information setting for the briefing’s proposed heavy-metal market position. Inferring that this creates an unoccupied category, willing buyers or a commercial advantage for HMTc is the author’s marketing interpretation, separate from the court holding and statutory obligations.

5.referenceTitle: Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind
5.citation: Ries, Al, and Jack Trout. Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind, 20th Anniversary Edition. McGraw Hill, ©2001, published 28 December 2000, ISBN 9780071359160. Ries, Al, and Jack Trout. The 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing. Harper Business, electronic edition, 13 October 2009. Ries, Laura. Visual Hammer: Nail Your Brand Into the Mind With the Emotional Power of a Visual Hammer. Laura Ries, 12 March 2012. Review limited to publisher descriptions, bibliographic records and contents listings.
5.summary: The publisher’s Positioning overview describes building a distinct place in a customer’s mind relative to competitors. The 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing draws practitioner lessons from campaigns judged successful or unsuccessful. Visual Hammer’s publisher description links a verbal brand position with a memorable visual. These are the three separate works grouped in this reference.
5.establishes: These sources supply marketing frameworks, not legal rules or an empirical forecast for heavy-metal certification. The reviewed material is limited to publisher overviews and contents; it does not verify every chapter-level paraphrase, prove that categories always acquire one owner, or establish the briefing’s claims about memory and consumer demand.
5.relevance: The briefing applies these frameworks to HMTc’s name, narrow subject and proposed visual identity. That application is the author’s strategy: the books do not evaluate HMTc, demonstrate that its market position is unclaimed, or establish that early adoption will generate a particular commercial return.

6.referenceTitle: HMTc Infant and Child Foods Program Manual
6.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. Heavy Metal Tested & Certified (HMTc) Infant and Child Foods Program Manual. 2026 edition, v0. The Paleo Foundation, 18 May 2026. doi:10.5281/zenodo.20270512. This is the cited first deposit; later editions supersede it.
6.summary: The cited 2026 v0 manual defines an infant-and-child-food program covering eight priority metals, with testing, surveillance, corrective action and certification-mark restrictions. Part 5.5 compares HMTc with USDA Organic, the Non-GMO Project, the Clean Label Project, EWG Healthy Living and Consumer Reports testing; this is the program author’s own comparison.
6.establishes: The manual describes HMTc’s declared scope and requirements. Parts 2.1 and 2.5 distinguish action levels from safety thresholds and prohibit claims of absolute safety, no metals or zero risk. Its comparison acknowledges other programs’ metal testing. It does not independently validate competitors’ scope, establish market priority, or show consumer recognition of HMTc.
6.relevance: It supplies the operational basis for the briefing’s focused claim: testing against published limits with ongoing surveillance. The analogy to the Butterfly, predictions of category ownership and assessment of HMTc’s visual identity remain positioning judgments. Because the cited deposit is superseded, current participation and mark-use decisions require the current manual.

1.referenceTitle: Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist
1.citation: Supreme Court of the United States. Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist, No. 24-724, 607 U.S. ___ (2026), decided 24 February 2026. Related factual and procedural history: Palmquist v. Hain Celestial Group, Inc., 103 F.4th 294 (5th Cir. 2024), No. 23-40197, decided 28 May 2024.
1.summary: The Supreme Court held that the erroneous dismissal of a retailer whose citizenship defeated federal diversity jurisdiction did not cure the jurisdictional defect. The Fifth Circuit opinion records the parents’ allegation that their son consumed Earth’s Best Organic products bought from Whole Foods.
1.establishes: These opinions establish the lawsuit’s procedural history and the allegations the courts considered. The Supreme Court’s holding concerns jurisdiction; it does not establish injury causation, product liability, or a failure of USDA organic certification.
1.relevance: The case supplies the family and product setting for this briefing’s discussion of expectations about organic food. The proposed role for HMTc is the author’s response to that setting, not a remedy ordered or validated by the Court.

2.referenceTitle: National Organic Program; Organic Foods Production Act of 1990
2.citation: United States. Organic Foods Production Act of 1990, Pub. L. 101-624, title XXI, 28 November 1990, 104 Stat. 3935, as amended, codified at 7 U.S.C. §§ 6501–6524 (2024 edition consulted). U.S. Department of Agriculture. National Organic Program, 7 C.F.R. Part 205, as amended (eCFR text current through 11 September 2026).
2.summary: The statute establishes national organic production and marketing standards; USDA’s regulations implement certification of production and handling operations, permitted inputs, inspections and labeling. Synthetic inputs are generally restricted, with specified National List exceptions.
2.establishes: These are legal requirements, but they do not provide a universal finished-food concentration certificate for lead, cadmium and arsenic. They do address contamination: § 205.203(c) expressly names heavy metals, and the statute and § 205.670 require residue testing and reporting of certain food-safety findings.
2.relevance: The rules support distinguishing production certification from HMTc’s proposed measurement against product-specific limits. That distinction should acknowledge organic contamination controls; it does not establish that organic certification never tests products or is wholly silent on heavy metals.

3.referenceTitle: Assessment of Heavy Metals in Organic and Non-Organic Vegetables Post Severe Tropical Cyclone Gabrielle: A cross-sectional comparative analysis
3.citation: Dearing, Chey; Ye, Zhijing; and Robertshaw, Glen. Assessment of Heavy Metals in Organic and Non-Organic Vegetables Post Severe Tropical Cyclone Gabrielle: A cross-sectional comparative analysis. F1000Research 14:1461 (26 December 2025), version 1, awaiting peer review in the examined version. doi:10.12688/f1000research.175538.1.
3.summary: This cross-sectional study tested 153 composite samples made from 736 vegetables bought at 14 Hawke’s Bay market gardens in February 2024. Its main analysis associated organic production with lower cadmium and nickel, and the authors reported four composite samples above their selected Codex limits.
3.establishes: The observations are local and do not establish a fertilizer mechanism or certification guarantee. Lead and arsenic were excluded from comparative statistical analysis because most results were below detection limits. In a 37-sample sensitivity analysis restricted by vegetable type, only nickel retained a significant organic association.
3.relevance: It supports discussing measured crop concentrations alongside organic status. For HMTc, the relevant distinction is between an observed group association and verified concentrations in a finished product; this study does not test U.S. organic certification or HMTc performance.

4.referenceTitle: Cadmium and Lead in Cocoa Powder and Chocolate Products in the U.S. Market
4.citation: Abt, Eileen; Fong Sam, Jennifer; Gray, Patrick; and Posnick Robin, Lauren. Cadmium and lead in cocoa powder and chocolate products in the US Market. Food Additives & Contaminants: Part B, Surveillance 11(2):92–102 (2018). doi:10.1080/19393210.2017.1420700.
4.summary: The authors’ abstract describes a convenience sample of U.S. retail cocoa powders, chocolate and cocoa nibs analyzed by ICP-MS. Cadmium and lead correlated with cocoa percentage; cadmium was higher in products with reported Latin American origins than African origins.
4.establishes: The accessible abstract supports variation by composition and reported origin in the sampled products. It does not establish an organic-versus-conventional comparison, a soil mechanism in those products, or a guarantee for any origin or certification. This review is limited to the authors’ abstract and bibliographic record.
4.relevance: The findings explain why product and sourcing evidence can matter when HMTc considers cocoa. They do not show that organic status is causally irrelevant or that HMTc certification reduces concentrations.

5.referenceTitle: Arsenic in Rice and Rice Products Risk Assessment
5.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Center for Food Safety and Applied Nutrition. Arsenic in Rice and Rice Products Risk Assessment Report, March 2016, version released for public comment. Related action-level document: Inorganic Arsenic in Rice Cereals for Infants: Action Level, Guidance for Industry, August 2020.
5.summary: The 2016 assessment models lifetime lung and bladder cancer risk from inorganic arsenic in rice and reviews potential effects during pregnancy and early childhood. FDA’s separate 2020 guidance recommends a 100 µg/kg (100 ppb) inorganic-arsenic action level for all infant rice cereals, including organically grown cereals.
5.establishes: The assessment explains rice uptake from soil and water under flooded conditions. It is a risk assessment, not itself the final action-level guidance. The 2020 recommendation is nonbinding and informs case-specific enforcement; its equal coverage of farming systems does not prove identical concentrations in them.
5.relevance: Together, these sources connect the briefing’s rice example to measured inorganic arsenic and product-specific controls. They support evaluating organic rice cereal against a contaminant benchmark while leaving HMTc’s own limits and certification requirements as separate program decisions.

6.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Total Diet Study Report: Fiscal Years 2018–2020 Elements Data. July 2022.
6.summary: FDA measured nutrient and contaminant elements in retail foods, generally prepared as consumed. The report documents detectable lead, arsenic, cadmium and mercury in portions of the sampled food supply, alongside many results below analytical detection limits.
6.establishes: This is national food surveillance, not an organic-versus-conventional comparison or testing of a particular brand’s compliance. Detection is not equivalent to harm, and a nondetect is not proof of absence. FDA does not take regulatory action from these composited TDS results.
6.relevance: The findings support the briefing’s restrained claims about measuring metals rather than promising their absence. They do not establish organic certification’s legal scope or show that every food contains detectable metals, and they do not validate HMTc’s effectiveness.

7.referenceTitle: HMTc Infant and Child Foods Program Manual
7.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. Heavy Metal Tested & Certified (HMTc) Infant and Child Foods Program Manual. 2026 edition, v0. The Paleo Foundation, 18 May 2026. doi:10.5281/zenodo.20270512. This cited first deposit has been superseded.
7.summary: The cited manual specifies HMTc’s product-testing and surveillance framework and restrictions on certification claims. Part 5.5 presents the program author’s comparison with USDA Organic and other schemes; Part 4 sets testing frequencies and laboratory requirements.
7.establishes: Parts 2.1 and 2.5 distinguish action levels from safety thresholds and prohibit absolute-safety, zero-metals and zero-risk claims. These are HMTc’s stated program rules, not government law, independent validation of other schemes, or evidence of a participating product’s actual performance.
7.relevance: It supplies the program specification for this briefing’s proposal to add measured heavy-metal evidence alongside organic certification. Whether a product meets that proposal requires its applicable current program requirements and testing records; the superseded manual alone supplies neither.

8.referenceTitle: Higher antioxidant and lower cadmium concentrations and lower incidence of pesticide residues in organically grown crops: a systematic literature review and meta-analyses
8.citation: Barański, Marcin; Średnicka-Tober, Dominika; Volakakis, Nikolaos; et al. Higher antioxidant and lower cadmium concentrations and lower incidence of pesticide residues in organically grown crops: a systematic literature review and meta-analyses. British Journal of Nutrition 112(5):794–811 (2014); first published online 15 July 2014. doi:10.1017/S0007114514001366.
8.summary: This review synthesized 343 publications comparing organic and conventional crops and crop-based foods; 156 provided information for weighted analyses. Both weighted and unweighted analyses found lower cadmium in organic crops overall. The authors detected no significant overall lead or arsenic difference.
8.establishes: These are pooled composition findings, not a metal-free guarantee or a test of human health outcomes. Results varied across crops and study methods. The authors discuss phosphorus fertilization, rotations and soil conditions as contributors, but could not quantify their relative contributions across the literature.
8.relevance: The review supports the briefing’s acknowledgment that organic growing can be associated with lower cadmium while leaving a separate role for product measurement. It does not establish that organic practices cannot affect soil-derived metals or that adding HMTc provides a demonstrated health benefit.

1.referenceTitle: Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist
1.citation: Supreme Court of the United States. Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist, No. 24-724, 607 U.S. ___ (2026), unanimous opinion by Justice Sotomayor, 24 February 2026. Below: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, Palmquist v. Hain Celestial Group, Inc., No. 23-40197, opinion by Judge Stewart, 28 May 2024.
1.summary: The Supreme Court affirmed that wrongly dismissing a retailer whose citizenship defeated federal diversity jurisdiction did not cure that defect. The manufacturer’s favorable federal judgment could not stand. The Fifth Circuit opinion supplies the underlying litigation and testing history.
1.establishes: The holding concerns jurisdiction, not product liability or certification. It does not bar every retailer dismissal, change the plaintiff’s burden to prove causation, or measure increases in defense costs, settlements or insurance premiums.
1.relevance: It explains why the briefing considers the financial consequences of losing a federal judgment. The five cost channels and proposed protection from HMTc are the author’s business analysis; they are not outcomes established by either court.

2.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Total Diet Study Report: Fiscal Years 2018–2020 Elements Data. July 2022.
2.summary: FDA’s national food-surveillance report measures nutrient and contaminant elements in retail foods, generally prepared as consumed. It documents detectable toxic elements across portions of the sampled food supply.
2.establishes: FDA reports detection in 15% of samples for lead, 43% for arsenic, 61% for cadmium and 8% for mercury. Composited surveillance results do not establish contamination in every product, an individual supplier’s violation, or any financial consequence.
2.relevance: The data support measuring metals rather than assuming their absence. They do not establish that a particular brand’s product almost certainly contains a detectable metal or quantify the cost of being uncertified.

3.referenceTitle: Litigation Cost Survey of Major Companies
3.citation: Lawyers for Civil Justice, Civil Justice Reform Group and U.S. Chamber Institute for Legal Reform. Litigation Cost Survey of Major Companies, May 2010. Survey administered by the Searle Center; submitted to the 2010 Conference on Civil Litigation.
3.summary: This industry-sponsored survey collected historical litigation expenses from major companies. It reports company averages for outside legal fees and discovery costs in major cases closed during 2004–2008.
3.establishes: The 2008 figures are approximately $2.02 million in outside fees and $622,000 in discovery costs. The selected large-company sample and major-case threshold limit generalization; this is a May 2010 industry survey, not a 2008 Federal Judicial Center study.
3.relevance: It supplies a historical benchmark for the briefing’s litigation model. It provides no estimate of post-Palmquist case frequency, settlement inflation or HMTc savings; annual expected cost still depends on separately justified probability and incremental-cost assumptions.

4.citation: Matching monetary record: Keep America Safe and Beautiful and Promix Nutrition, Inc., Settlement and Release Agreement, fully executed 24 November 2024; California Attorney General Proposition 65 notice no. 2024-02424, recorded as KASB v. Promix Nutrition, Inc., out-of-court settlement. The bibliography’s People v. Promix Nutrition consent-judgment identification was not verified.
4.summary: The official record matching the cited company and exact $28,000 allocation is a private settlement over alleged lead-warning violations involving Promix Lemon Pre-Workout. It is recorded as KASB v. Promix, rather than the People v. Promix consent judgment named here.
4.establishes: The agreement assigns $3,000 to a civil penalty and $25,000 to the claimant’s legal, expert and investigation costs. Promix denies violations. The agreement requires specified warnings for covered exposure levels; it does not establish liability, actual reformulation or the company’s total costs.
4.relevance: It illustrates how a warning dispute can include substantial claimant-side fees. A single 2024 settlement involving a pre-workout product cannot establish baby-food settlement values, changes caused by Palmquist, or savings attributable to HMTc.

5.referenceTitle: Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury
5.citation: U.S. House of Representatives, Committee on Oversight and Reform, Subcommittee on Economic and Consumer Policy. Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury. Staff report, 4 February 2021.
5.summary: Congressional staff examined manufacturer documents and criticized ingredient-only testing. The report describes Hain’s 2019 presentation showing that finished rice products could contain more inorganic arsenic than estimates based on ingredient testing.
5.establishes: It documents the staff’s findings and recommendations, rather than a judicial determination of negligence or causation. It does not measure how juries value testing records or how certification changes financial losses.
5.relevance: The report supports the briefing’s concern about relying solely on ingredient records. HMTc’s case for finished-product verification draws on that concern; the proposed litigation advantage remains an inference.

6.citation: California Assembly Bill 899, Chapter 668, Statutes of 2023, adding Health and Safety Code §§110962–110963. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, Assembly Bill 899 – Food Safety: Baby Food, enforcement advisory to manufacturers and retailers, 6 March 2026.
6.summary: AB 899 requires testing and public disclosure for defined baby foods sold in California, with testing phased in during 2024 and disclosure in 2025. The March 2026 advisory explains those duties and warns manufacturers and retailers about enforcement.
6.establishes: The statute creates legal obligations within its defined scope, excluding infant formula. The advisory communicates the Attorney General’s enforcement position; it does not create a new certification requirement or establish measured increases in litigation or insurance costs.
6.relevance: These are concrete compliance costs behind the briefing’s balance-sheet argument. HMTc documentation can support compliance work, but a private certificate does not replace the manufacturer’s statutory testing, disclosure and applicable labeling duties.

7.referenceTitle: ISO/IEC 17025:2017, General Requirements for the Competence of Testing and Calibration Laboratories
7.citation: International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission. ISO/IEC 17025:2017, General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories. Third edition, November 2017; confirmed in 2023.
7.summary: ISO/IEC 17025 describes general requirements for laboratory competence, impartiality and consistent operation. The official overview explains its use for testing and calibration laboratories and accreditation.
7.establishes: This is a laboratory standard, not certification of a food product or a guarantee that testing will defeat a lawsuit. Only ISO’s public overview was reviewed; the paid normative standard and any individual laboratory’s accreditation scope were not accessed.
7.relevance: It supports the competence and impartiality requirements behind the briefing’s proposed independent testing evidence. Appropriate laboratory scope, methods, sampling and product-specific decisions still need verification; the overview does not prove litigation savings.

8.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. Heavy Metal Tested & Certified (HMTc) Infant and Child Foods Program Manual. 2026 edition, v0. The Paleo Foundation, 18 May 2026. doi:10.5281/zenodo.20270512. This is the cited first deposit; later editions supersede it.

9.referenceTitle: The Cost of Operating Without Credible Third-Party Heavy-Metal Certification
9.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. The Cost of Operating Without Credible Third-Party Heavy-Metal Certification. Journal of Food Metallomics, preprint, 7 March 2026, pp. 1–6. doi: 10.5281/zenodo.18903738.
9.summary: This author-produced preprint combines recall, litigation and market anchors into illustrative one-year loss scenarios: $1.6M–$6.6M+ at $5M revenue, $8M–$33M+ at $50M, and $57M–$187M+ at $500M, in section 7.3.

1.referenceTitle: Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist
1.citation: Supreme Court of the United States. Hain Celestial Group, Inc. v. Palmquist, No. 24-724, 607 U.S. ___ (2026), decided 24 February 2026. Opinion of Justice Sotomayor for a unanimous Court. Related HMTc commentary: K. Pendergrass, After Palmquist (2026).
1.summary: The Supreme Court reviewed whether a federal judgment could stand after a retailer sharing the plaintiffs’ state citizenship had been wrongly dismissed from a baby-food lawsuit. The accompanying HMTc briefing discusses implications for manufacturers and retailers.
1.establishes: The dismissal did not cure the federal court’s lack of jurisdiction, so the judgment in Hain’s favor could not stand. The decision resolved which court could hear the dispute; it did not establish that the food caused injury or that either company was liable.
1.relevance: It provides the legal setting for this briefing’s discussion of brand trust and product evidence. HMTc’s case for verification is a program interpretation; the ruling does not require certification or show that certification prevents lawsuits.

2.referenceTitle: Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury
2.citation: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Reform, Subcommittee on Economic and Consumer Policy. Staff report, 4 February 2021.
2.summary: Congressional staff examined company testing records for arsenic, lead, cadmium and mercury in baby foods and recommended finished-product testing and public disclosure.
2.establishes: The report describes Hain's reliance on ingredient testing and an August 2019 presentation of finished-product results. It does not establish when finished-product testing first began.
2.relevance: It supports the briefing's distinction between brand trust and product verification. Its evidence is narrower than the claim that testing began only in 2019, and does not resolve whether a product caused an individual child's injury.

3.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Total Diet Study Report: Fiscal Years 2018–2020 Elements Data. July 2022.
3.summary: FDA measured nutrient and contaminant elements in retail foods, generally prepared for consumption. Its national monitoring results document detectable arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury in parts of the food supply.
3.establishes: These are food-surveillance data, not a comparison of organic and conventional farming or verification of a particular brand. A nondetect means below the analytical reporting limit, not demonstrated absence. FDA does not take regulatory action from these composited TDS results.
3.relevance: The findings support this briefing's case for measured product evidence and carefully bounded claims. They cannot establish an organic label's scope, prove all foods contain detectable metals, or endorse HMTc certification.

4.citation: International Food Information Council. 2025 IFIC Food & Health Survey: A Focus On Food & Ingredient Safety. July 2025. Also: Yi, Rachael. Trust in Government Assurance of Food Safety Hits Record Low. Gallup, 6 September 2024; Brenan, Megan. U.S. Confidence in Institutions Mostly Flat, but Police Up. Gallup, 15 July 2024.
4.summary: IFIC's 2025 survey found declining food-safety confidence and heavy metals among consumers' concerns. Gallup's separate 2024 poll found 57% confident in federal food-safety assurance and 72% confident in grocery-store food safety; its institutional survey reported a 28% average across 14 institutions.
4.establishes: These surveys measure reported attitudes using different questions and dates. IFIC's confidence rating and its separate question about improving confidence are distinct measures. None tests food contamination, quantifies premium-brand losses, or demonstrates that certification restores trust.
4.relevance: They give the briefing context for explaining verification clearly to skeptical consumers. HMTc's proposed response is a program decision; these findings do not establish consumer preference for HMTc or a financial return from certification.

5.referenceTitle: The Counterproductive Consequences of Public Exposé Testing: How Unstructured Disclosure Undermines Heavy Metal Contamination Reduction
5.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. The Counterproductive Consequences of Public Exposé Testing: How Unstructured Disclosure Undermines Heavy Metal Contamination Reduction. Journal of Food Metallomics, preprint, 8 April 2026. doi: 10.5281/zenodo.19470572.
5.summary: Pendergrass argues that selective public testing without category benchmarks, repeated sampling or measurement uncertainty can discourage disclosure and burden small brands investing in quality. The paper proposes supplier intelligence, structured testing and confidential remediation as alternatives.
5.establishes: This is a preprint by the briefing’s author, explicitly marked as not yet peer reviewed. It develops an argument from existing literature and examples; it does not measure how often premium brands are targeted or establish a causal effect of exposés on contamination reduction.
5.relevance: It supplies the reasoning behind this briefing’s account of unequal reputational exposure. HMTc’s proposed response is continuing verification with interpretable results and improvement pathways. The source does not prove that premium brands are always targeted first.

6.referenceTitle: The Cost of Operating Without Credible Third-Party Heavy-Metal Certification
6.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. The Cost of Operating Without Credible Third-Party Heavy-Metal Certification. Journal of Food Metallomics, preprint, 7 March 2026, pp. 1–6. doi: 10.5281/zenodo.18903738.
6.summary: This paper combines contamination, recall, litigation and retailer evidence in illustrative business-loss scenarios. Section 7.3 estimates first-year costs of $1.6M–$6.6M or more for a $5M-revenue brand experiencing a public heavy-metals event, including recall, legal, sales, distribution and remediation costs.
6.establishes: These are modeled scenarios by the briefing’s author, not observed losses for a representative group of premium brands. The model assumes incident severity, sales disruption and certification benefits; it does not independently measure how much HMTc reduces event risk or establish a guaranteed return.
6.relevance: It provides the scenario behind this briefing’s financial-exposure example and a framework for weighing verification costs against potential disruption. A brand would need its own incident probability, margins, channel exposure and program costs to assess the business case.

7.referenceTitle: HMTc Infant and Child Foods Program Manual
7.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. Heavy Metal Tested & Certified (HMTc) Infant and Child Foods Program Manual. 2026 edition, v0. The Paleo Foundation, 18 May 2026. doi:10.5281/zenodo.20270512. This is the cited first deposit; later editions supersede it.
7.summary: The manual specifies HMTc’s infant-food certification framework: product testing, surveillance, corrective action and restrictions on use of the certification mark. The cited edition also compares the program with USDA Organic, Non-GMO Project and other certification or testing programs.
7.establishes: Parts 2.1 and 2.5 treat action levels as tools for managing contamination and prohibit claims of absolute safety, zero metals or zero risk. These are HMTc program requirements, not government law or independent evidence that certification prevents injury, litigation or loss of consumer trust.
7.relevance: It supplies the program rules behind this briefing’s argument for making verifiable claims: describe testing against stated limits and continuing surveillance, while avoiding a promise of safety. Its comparison of certification scopes explains why an organic or non-GMO badge cannot stand in for verification of metal concentrations.

1.referenceTitle: Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury
1.citation: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Reform, Subcommittee on Economic and Consumer Policy. Staff report, 4 February 2021.
1.summary: Congressional staff examined company testing records for arsenic, lead, cadmium and mercury in baby foods and recommended finished-product testing and public disclosure.
1.establishes: It documents the investigation's four-metal scope. It does not establish a complete testing panel, industry-wide certification practice or subsequent litigation history.
1.relevance: It grounds the briefing's opening discussion of the familiar four metals. The later claim about multidistrict litigation needs a separate court source; the case for testing additional elements rests on the other cited assessments and standards.

1.referenceTitle: Heavy Metal Tested & Certified (HMTc) Infant and Child Foods Program Manual
1.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. Heavy Metal Tested & Certified (HMTc) Infant and Child Foods Program Manual. 2026 edition, v0. The Paleo Foundation, 18 May 2026. doi:10.5281/zenodo.20270512. This is the cited first deposit; later editions supersede it.
1.summary: The manual describes HMTc’s product certification rules, including testing, status changes, remediation, mark use, appeals and disclosure of conflicts. It is the program operator’s primary account of the obligations and limits discussed throughout this primer.
1.establishes: It establishes what the cited edition says the program requires, rather than independently proving the program’s effectiveness. This May 2026 v0 deposit is superseded: its conditional permission for Status B mark use differs from the primer’s A-only description.
1.relevance: It is the main source for assessing the program described here, including the distinction between action levels and safety guarantees and the limits of remediation confidentiality. Version-specific rules should be checked against the current manual and executed agreement before relying on eligibility or obligations.

2.referenceTitle: The Counterproductive Consequences of Public Exposé Testing
2.citation: Pendergrass, Karen. Three Journal of Food Metallomics preprints: The Counterproductive Consequences of Public Exposé Testing: How Unstructured Disclosure Undermines Heavy Metal Contamination Reduction (8 April 2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.19470572; The Cost of Operating Without Credible Third-Party Heavy-Metal Certification (7 March 2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.18903738; and Certification as a Framework for Reducing Heavy Metal Exposure in Infant and Child Foods: Integrating Legal Defensibility, Scientific Rigor, and Commercial Viability (8 March 2026), doi:10.5281/zenodo.18905821.
2.summary: These three preprints by the program’s architect argue for structured testing and remediation, model potential business losses, and propose staged certification with repeated measurement and progressively tighter standards. They provide the conceptual background for the program described in this primer.
2.establishes: The papers present design arguments and illustrative scenarios, not independent trials measuring HMTc’s effect on exposure or litigation costs. Their deposit as preprints does not establish peer review or validate the current software that calculates program limits.
2.relevance: They explain the reasoning behind combining testing, improvement pathways and commercial incentives. They should be read alongside the manual: the framework preprint describes an earlier limit-setting approach and does not independently establish the primer’s later calculation method.

3.referenceTitle: General Requirements for the Competence of Testing and Calibration Laboratories
3.citation: International Organization for Standardization and International Electrotechnical Commission. ISO/IEC 17025:2017, General requirements for the competence of testing and calibration laboratories. Third edition, November 2017; confirmed in 2023.
3.summary: ISO/IEC 17025 sets a common benchmark for laboratory competence, impartiality and consistent operation. Accreditation bodies use the standard when assessing testing and calibration laboratories.
3.establishes: The standard concerns laboratory performance; it does not itself certify a food product or establish HMTc’s contaminant limits. The public ISO description confirms its purpose, but does not show whether any particular laboratory holds suitable accreditation.
3.relevance: It explains the laboratory competence requirement in HMTc’s testing lifecycle. Relevant accreditation and analytical methods still need checking for each laboratory; HMTc’s sampling schedule, certification statuses and chosen decision rule come from the program’s own requirements.

1.referenceTitle: Baby Foods Are Tainted with Dangerous Levels of Arsenic, Lead, Cadmium, and Mercury
1.citation: U.S. House Committee on Oversight and Reform, Subcommittee on Economic and Consumer Policy. Staff report, 4 February 2021.
1.summary: Congressional staff reviewed manufacturers’ testing records and reported arsenic, lead, cadmium and mercury contamination in baby foods, alongside weaknesses in testing and internal company limits.
1.establishes: The report recommended finished-product testing, regulatory limits and public disclosure. It was an investigation of company records, not an independent testing study or an enacted safety standard.
1.relevance: It provides context for HMTc’s emphasis on finished-product verification and the familiar four-metal panel. Its scope does not establish that only those four elements warrant testing.

2.referenceTitle: Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food
2.citation: European Commission. Regulation (EU) 2023/915, 25 April 2023. Original act, OJ L 119, 5 May 2023; Annex I, section 3.5.
2.summary: This regulation consolidates EU maximum contaminant levels for specified foods. Its metal provisions include inorganic tin in canned products, alongside lead, cadmium, arsenic and mercury.
2.establishes: The original act sets binding tin limits that distinguish general canned foods, beverages and specified infant foods. The applicable food category and exclusions matter; it is not a universal limit for all foods.
2.relevance: It provides a regulatory basis for including tin in HMTc’s coverage and matching limits to product and packaging. Applying a category’s limit elsewhere requires a separate, disclosed HMTc decision.

3.referenceTitle: Commission Regulation (EU) 2024/1987 amending Regulation (EU) 2023/915 as regards maximum levels of nickel in food
3.citation: European Commission. Regulation (EU) 2024/1987, 30 July 2024. Published 31 July 2024; Annex, section 3.6.
3.summary: This amendment introduces nickel maximum levels for specified foods in response to EFSA’s assessment of dietary exposure and health risks.
3.establishes: The legal limits distinguish food categories, including powdered formula, qualifying soy-isolate formula and liquid formula. Most apply from July 2025, with specified cereal provisions applying from July 2026.
3.relevance: This is the concentration-limit source behind the briefing’s inclusion of nickel and its formula distinctions. EFSA’s assessment in reference 7 explains the health rationale; this regulation supplies the food-specific legal requirements.

4.referenceTitle: Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code — Schedule 19, Maximum levels of contaminants and natural toxicants
4.citation: Food Standards Australia New Zealand. Schedule 19, compilation 6, 13 September 2024; infant-formula changes under Proposal P1028.
4.summary: Schedule 19 includes tin limits for canned foods and separate aluminium limits for infant-formula categories, extending food-contaminant controls beyond the conventional four metals.
4.establishes: The aluminium entries distinguish general, soy-based and specified preterm formula. The revised infant-formula rules apply in Australia with transition arrangements through September 2029; New Zealand opted out of those revisions.
4.relevance: These provisions support considering aluminium and tin in HMTc’s panel. Any use of the formula benchmark in another category must identify the jurisdiction, edition, preparation basis and rationale for that application.

5.citation: California Assembly Bill 899. Chapter 668, Statutes of 2023, approved 10 October 2023; Health and Safety Code sections 110962–110963.
5.summary: AB 899 requires covered baby-food manufacturers to test finished products for arsenic, cadmium, lead and mercury at least monthly, and to disclose product results publicly.
5.establishes: Testing began in January 2024 and public disclosure in January 2025. The law covers specified foods for children under two, excludes infant formula, and does not itself set numerical maximum metal concentrations.
5.relevance: It is a concrete example of a mandatory four-element disclosure panel. HMTc’s broader testing scope is a program decision; the law’s four-element list does not establish that other metals are irrelevant.

6.referenceTitle: Action Levels for Lead in Processed Food Intended for Babies and Young Children: Guidance for Industry
6.citation: U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Final guidance for industry, January 2025, issued 6 January 2025.
6.summary: FDA’s Closer to Zero guidance sets lead action levels for specified processed foods marketed for children under two, with different levels for different food categories.
6.establishes: These action levels inform FDA’s decisions about adulteration alongside other evidence. They are nonbinding recommendations, not universal safety thresholds; infant formula, beverages and snacks such as puffs are outside this guidance’s scope.
6.relevance: The guidance supports HMTc’s use of category-specific controls and careful identification of regulatory scope. It addresses lead in the named foods, rather than establishing a comprehensive metal-testing panel.

7.referenceTitle: Update of the Risk Assessment of Nickel in Food and Drinking Water
7.citation: EFSA CONTAM Panel. EFSA Journal 2020;18(11):6268, published 5 November 2020. DOI: 10.2903/j.efsa.2020.6268.
7.summary: EFSA reassessed dietary nickel using updated toxicology and food-occurrence data. It identified concerns for children with high exposure and for people already sensitized to nickel.
7.establishes: The chronic intake benchmark rests on reproductive effects in rats. High dietary exposure raised concern in young age groups, while acute oral exposure can provoke eczema in sensitized people. These are distinct health endpoints, not interchangeable thresholds.
7.relevance: This assessment provides the dietary-health rationale for including nickel in HMTc’s panel. The food concentration limits and formula distinctions discussed in the briefing come from the separate EU regulation in reference 3.

8.referenceTitle: IARC Monographs on the Identification of Carcinogenic Hazards to Humans
8.citation: International Agency for Research on Cancer. Monographs, volume 49 (1990) and volume 100C (2012); nickel chapter, volume 100C, pp. 169–218.
8.summary: IARC evaluates carcinogenic hazards using human, animal and mechanistic evidence. These volumes cover nickel compounds and other metals relevant to the briefing.
8.establishes: Nickel compounds are classified as carcinogenic to humans. The human evidence concerns lung and nasal cancers in occupationally exposed populations; the classification does not quantify cancer risk from eating nickel-containing foods.
8.relevance: The monographs provide hazard context for HMTc’s panel and show why chemical form and exposure route matter. Dietary nickel risk is addressed more directly by EFSA in reference 7; an IARC classification does not set a food limit.

9.referenceTitle: General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed (CXS 193-1995), tin maximum levels
9.citation: Codex Alimentarius Commission (FAO/WHO). General Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and Feed, CXS 193-1995, amended 2025; tin provisions.
9.summary: Codex’s general contaminant standard includes maximum tin levels for canned foods and canned beverages, with the two categories treated separately.
9.establishes: Tin is an established food-contaminant concern in international standards. These are commodity-specific Codex levels; they do not automatically become domestic law or apply to every food.
9.relevance: This supports HMTc’s inclusion of tin beyond the four-metal convention and its attention to packaging. HMTc must still compare applicable national requirements and select the correct product category when deriving a limit.

10.referenceTitle: Evaluation of Certain Food Additives and Contaminants (aluminium; tin)
10.citation: JECFA. Aluminium: 74th meeting, WHO TRS 966 (2011). Tin: 33rd meeting (1988), TRS 776 (1989); later clarification at the 64th meeting (2005), TRS 930 (2006).
10.summary: This reference combines separate assessments. Aluminium is evaluated through cumulative dietary intake; tin’s principal canned-food concern is acute gastrointestinal irritation.
10.establishes: The aluminium evaluation derives a provisional weekly intake benchmark. Later tin evaluations emphasize that irritation depends on the concentration and nature of tin in the product, and can occur around existing canned-product limits in some people.
10.relevance: These assessments support treating aluminium exposure and tin contamination differently within HMTc. They do not independently establish HMTc’s aluminium limits for other food categories, or make an elevated tin result a definitive diagnosis of can failure.

11.referenceTitle: Scientific Opinion: Safety of Aluminium from Dietary Intake
11.citation: EFSA AFC Panel. EFSA Journal 2008;6(7):754, pp. 1–34, published 15 July 2008. DOI: 10.2903/j.efsa.2008.754.
11.summary: EFSA assessed aluminium exposure from food, accounting for its persistence in the body and adverse effects observed in animal studies. Estimated dietary exposure could exceed its tolerable intake in part of the European population.
11.establishes: The opinion sets a health-based reference for total weekly dietary exposure. It addresses cumulative intake, rather than prescribing a maximum aluminium concentration for an individual food.
11.relevance: It explains why aluminium warrants attention in HMTc’s broader panel. Deriving an HMTc product limit still requires a separate rationale that connects exposure, food category and the chosen regulatory benchmark.

12.referenceTitle: IRIS Toxicological Review of Hexavalent Chromium [Cr(VI)]
12.citation: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. EPA/635/R-24/164Fa, August 2024; released 12 August 2024.
12.summary: EPA reviewed the cancer and noncancer effects of hexavalent chromium and concluded that it is likely to be carcinogenic to humans through oral exposure.
12.establishes: The assessment characterizes hazards and dose-response relationships specifically for Cr(VI). Its oral noncancer reference dose rests on small-intestine effects in mice; it is not a food concentration limit or an assessment of total chromium as one substance.
12.relevance: It supports distinguishing chromium species when HMTc interprets a total-chromium result. The choice of a screening trigger and the resulting certification decision remain HMTc program rules with their own justification.

13.referenceTitle: EFSA CONTAM Panel scientific opinions on lead, arsenic, mercury, and cadmium in food
13.summary: These five opinions assess dietary exposure and critical health effects for lead, inorganic arsenic, mercury species and cadmium. They are separate assessments with different endpoints and methods.
13.establishes: Lead and inorganic arsenic are assessed using benchmark reference points and exposure comparisons; mercury and cadmium have tolerable weekly intakes. Chemical form matters, particularly for arsenic and mercury.
13.relevance: The opinions support retaining the original four contaminants within HMTc’s broader panel and identifying relevant chemical species. They provide the scientific basis for concern, while HMTc separately defines its tiers, product limits and certification rules.

14.citation: NSF/ANSI 173-2025, Dietary Supplements. NSF / American National Standards Institute.
14.summary: NSF/ANSI 173 addresses dietary-supplement identity, declared composition and contaminants. NSF’s public certification description names lead, arsenic, cadmium, mercury and chromium(VI) among the toxic contaminants evaluated.
14.establishes: This is a documented supplement-certification comparator whose published screening scope extends beyond the familiar four metals. The public scope description identifies contaminants, rather than supplying the full standard’s numerical requirements.
14.relevance: It gives HMTc a specific basis for comparing the contaminants named by another program. Claims of unique or broader market coverage require a separate, current comparison of all relevant programs.

15.referenceTitle: ICH Q3D Guideline for Elemental Impurities; USP General Chapter <232>
15.citation: ICH Q3D(R2), adopted 26 April 2022. USP General Chapter <232>, Elemental Impurities—Limits; implementation FAQ, 27 March 2015 (chapter revision unspecified).
15.summary: ICH Q3D provides a risk-based framework and permitted daily exposures for elemental impurities in drug products. USP chapter <232> addresses elemental-impurity limits in that pharmaceutical context.
15.establishes: ICH’s table overlaps seven Big 8 element names and omits an aluminium exposure limit. Its default chromium assessment concerns Cr(III), with Cr(VI) requiring separate consideration; listed elements do not all require testing in every product.
15.relevance: The pharmaceutical framework offers a comparison of scope and exposure-based limits. Its element-name overlap is not equivalent to HMTc’s chemical-species coverage, food standards or testing requirements.
